analysis.one_liner: Phases out for-profit contractors from federal prisons and halfway houses and adds reentry help for released prisoners.
analysis.headline: The bill has sat in the House Judiciary Committee since its May 2025 introduction, with no hearing, markup, or floor vote scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would bar the federal Bureau of Prisons and the Marshals Service from hiring private, for-profit companies to run prisons and halfway houses, with phase-outs over six to eight years. It would also require annual inspections of jails holding federal detainees, periodic reports on who is in federal custody, and new services for people leaving federal prison — help with food assistance, Medicaid, ID, and registering to vote. It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and has not moved since.
analysis.who_benefits: People held in federal prisons and jails — including pretrial detainees in Marshals Service custody — and their families, who would be housed in facilities run by public employees instead of companies that profit from cutting costs. People leaving federal prison would also gain from guaranteed information and counseling on benefits, jobs, records, and voting. Taxpayers could gain from ending profit margins on incarceration, though the record does not quantify that.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Federal prisoners, detainees, and their families

how_it_helps.text: Six years after enactment, all core correctional services at federal Bureau of Prisons and Marshals Service facilities must be performed by federal employees, ending for-profit operation of federal prisons; state and local government facilities remain allowed if they meet all standards.

Eight years after enactment, the Bureau of Prisons may no longer contract with for-profit entities to provide or manage community confinement facilities (halfway houses), and the Attorney General must phase out existing contracts.
Released federal prisoners must receive information and counseling on expungement rights, job programs, food assistance, Medicaid, Social Security, driver's licenses, and voter registration.
The Marshals Service must annually inspect every facility it uses to confine people in its custody, to verify constitutional, federal, state, and local standards are met.

The Attorney General must report to Congress every two years on the federal prison population, including race, gender, age, and nationality, and must research which community confinement programs reduce recidivism.

analysis.who_pays: For-profit prison and halfway-house companies would lose federal contracts and revenue over the transition. The federal government would need to hire staff or arrange public capacity to take over contracted facilities, a cost the bill does not estimate. Some counties that host private facilities serving the Marshals Service could lose those contracts unless they run the facilities with government employees.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private prison companies and federal corrections budgets

drawbacks.text: The phase-out is long: private companies could keep operating federal prisons for six years and halfway houses for eight years after enactment, so the change would not be immediate.
The bill sets no funding or cost estimate for hiring federal staff or arranging replacement capacity, so taxpayers would bear transition costs that are not quantified in the bill text.
State and local government facilities may still contract with the Marshals Service, so government-run — though not privately run — contracting continues.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core change — removing profit from operating federal prisons — addresses conditions that reformers have long criticized, and the reentry and inspection provisions add real services at modest cost. The main honest objections are the multi-year timeline that keeps private operators in place during the transition and the unbudgeted cost of shifting to federal staff. On balance the bill's benefits for incarcerated people and their families are concrete, while its costs are real but deferred and unquantified.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in May 2025 and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, which has taken no action on it since.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the House on May 23, 2025, by Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman with five original cosponsors, and was referred the same day to the House Committee on the Judiciary.
The House Judiciary Committee has held no markup, hearing, or vote on the bill, and no further action appears in the record after the referral.
The bill has 6 cosponsors, all House Democrats.

The bill would amend federal law to require that core correctional services at Bureau of Prisons and Marshals Service facilities be performed by government employees after a six-year transition, and would ban Bureau of Prisons contracts with for-profit community confinement facilities after eight years.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: For now, private prison and halfway-house companies keep their federal contracts, since no phase-out has been enacted. The bill's sponsors and the people it would protect are waiting on a committee that has not acted.

for.name: Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the House Judiciary Committee.

for.name: 6 of 217 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican cosponsored it.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by a Republican
against.what_they_did: Received the referral in May 2025 and has taken no action — no markup, hearing, or vote — since.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Has not brought the bill to the House floor; with a Republican majority and no committee action, no vote has been scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: All six cosponsors are Democrats and no Republican has sponsored or cosponsored the bill; no vote has occurred, so no roll-call split exists.

industries.industry: Private prison and detention contractors (e.g. CoreCivic, GEO Group)
industries.note: The bill phases out their Bureau of Prisons and Marshals Service contracts for running prisons and halfway houses, removing the profit margin from federal incarceration. These companies have long depended on federal detention revenue, so the bill directly targets their business model.

After an eight-year transition, the Bureau of Prisons could no longer contract with for-profit entities to provide or manage halfway houses, and existing contracts must be phased out. These operators currently hold the federal reentry contracts the bill would end.

analysis.trajectory: Bills referred to the House Judiciary Committee typically need the committee to hold a markup before any floor vote, and with a Republican majority, no cosponsors from the majority party, and no action for months, this bill is very likely to stay in committee for the rest of this Congress unless advocates force a separate vehicle, such as attaching the provision to a broader justice or spending bill.
